## Intent

The PoC does not prove the claim: a tautological assertion, a simulator or mock instead of the real contract, or no failing assertion at all. The finding may be true; the evidence is not evidence.

## Detection signals

Signals are the tautology shapes (an assertion that a value is at least zero, which no unsigned value can fail) and mock/simulator class names. The default verdict is a NOTE, not a kill: naming a mock is ordinary PoC scaffolding. It becomes a hard fail only when the report says the mock stood in for the real thing, and ordinary scaffolding names are dropped outright before the rule is even considered.

Patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions matched against the full text of the
draft finding, subject to the engine rules below.

**Fires when at least one of these matches:**

```text
  assert!\(\s*\w+\s*>=\s*0\s*\)
  assert\(\s*\w+\s*>=\s*0\s*\)
  (?-i:\b(Mock|Simulator|Fake|Stub)[A-Z]\w*)
  imports? a (mock|simulator)
```

**Escalates.** A match on any of these strong forms raises the rule to `hard`, because these are the forms that name the
problem rather than hedge around it:

```text
  instead of the real (contract|implementation|deployment)
  simulates? the (contract|protocol|behaviou?r)
  not the (real|deployed|in-scope) contract
  mock(ed)? (the )?(contract|implementation) rather than
```

**Dropped.** A match on any of these is discarded outright, so the rule does not fire
at all. This is how the rule stops firing on ordinary scaffolding:

```text
  (?-i:\bMock(ERC20|Token|Vault|Router|Pair|Factory)\b)
  (?-i:\bStub[A-Z]\w*\b)
```

## Escape hatches

Two mechanisms rather than a suppression list. A DOWNGRADE list drops the ordinary scaffolding names (a standard mock token, a stub class) before the rule fires at all. An ESCALATION list raises the rule to a hard fail when the report admits the mock stood in for the real contract. A defective PoC is fixed by rewriting it, not by rewording the finding.

## Known false-positive modes

These are the shapes where the rule fires on something it should not. They are the
reason a firing is a prompt to check, not a verdict.

- A PoC that uses a mock for a *peripheral* dependency while exercising the real in-scope contract.
- A finding whose PoC is a runnable script rather than a test, so the assertion patterns do not apply.
- A report that quotes a mock's name while describing the target's own interface.

## Synthetic examples

Both examples are synthetic. They describe no real report and no real target.

**Fires:** "The PoC imports a MockVault and its only assertion is that a balance is greater than or equal to zero."

**Does not fire:** "The PoC imports the real in-scope contract and asserts the delta."

## Corrective action

Rewrite the PoC to (a) import the real in-scope contract, (b) assert the harmful state delta, and (c) resolve every path against a fresh clone at the exact commit.

| 2026-10-10 | Default verdict is now a note rather than a kill, and ordinary scaffolding names are dropped outright. Naming a mock is not evidence that the PoC is defective; only an admission that the mock stood in for the real contract escalates the rule. |
